The states' attorneys general are seeking civil penalties, fees and to make SpaceX put stricter guardrails in place. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty Images Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator. Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others. In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material. The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content. Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images. "This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation." In a statement emailed to CNBC by a spokesperson for SpaceXSI, and posted on the company's @Safety account on X, the company said, "When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement. Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors." At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products. SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California. In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction. When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content. SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions." The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company. Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance. State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms. In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online. headlines.article_text: Tokenized stocks face pushback as NYSE, Nasdaq pivot for a new market Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points OKXICE launches Monday with Coinbase, Robinhood, Strategy, Circle, Securitize and BitGo will be available to trade in tokenized form. Most of the 62 companies initially targeted objected to having their shares tokenized on the platform, likely reflecting a lack of preparedness versus a rejection of tokenization. Company objections raise a separate question about which of the different tokenization models will prove most attractive. In this article ICE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, Nov. 10, 2026. Angela Weiss | AFP | Getty Images OKXICE, a trading platform for tokenized securities jointly operated by Intercontinental Exchange and crypto exchange OKX, is set to debut Monday despite objections from 90% of the companies whose stocks it initially proposed to list. Of the 62 companies whose shares OKXICE first sought to trade, 56 objected to having their shares tokenized and traded on the platform, according to a review of public notices posted between Oct. 4 and Nov. 5 . By last week, even more companies had objected , including those not on the original roster. The high objection rate may reflect companies' lack of readiness to have blockchain-based representations of their shares traded on a new third-party platform like OKXICE, rather than broad resistance to tokenization. People involved in talks with some of the companies say a 30-day objection window left them little time to react and decide if they were ready to participate. 'Revolutionary,' 'transformational' "The shift to a 24/7 global marketplace is revolutionary and transformational for our market structure," Andrew Cuomo, co-chair of OKXICE, told CNBC. "The majority of companies aren't familiar with [tokenization] and haven't had a chance to understand it and the consequences." "Logic dictates that many companies were going to be cautious before they understood what the system would do," added Cuomo, who served 10 years as governor of New York until 2021. "What you're seeing now is the more the companies learn about 24/7 global access, the more receptive they are." At launch, tokenized shares of Coinbase , Robinhood , Strategy , Circle , Securitize and BitGo will be available to trade on the platform, OKXICE disclosed in a public notice. OKXICE has confirmed 113 assets, including exchange-traded funds and products, going live on a rolling basis. Since its initial pre-launch announcement on Nov. 11, OKXICE said it's seen further interest from different issuers and Fidelity Investments , Direxion, eToro , Strive and Vida Global are now participating. The 30-day opt-out window is a requirement of the SEC's so-called Innovation Exemption , which took effect in September and temporarily permits the trading of certain tokenized stocks. Under the exemption, trading platforms must notify the underlying issuers and give them an opportunity to object. Any issuer who objects blocks its shares from being tokenized. "We've gotten a lot of feedback that the reason why you've seen this high number of rejections of tokenizing equity is because it was a 30-day window," Seth Ginns, chief investment officer at Franklin Templeton's crypto arm, told CNBC at the Digital Assets Forum in New York earlier this month. Many issuers were open to exploring the idea but were hesitant to move forward amid competing priorities, he said. "[They're] saying it's earnings season, there was the midterms, there's a lot going on during this 30-day window. Give us some time, we want to learn about it, we're not closed to the idea we're just closed to rushing into it right now," Ginns added. Announcement timing Ran Grushkowsky, CEO of MassPay, a global payout platform, said several of his company's clients were among the initial targets and shared that their concern was less about the concept of tokenization and more about how 24/7 trading could affect stock value and investor relations strategies, particularly around the timing of corporate announcements. "It's more [about] what's going to be the effect, how is it going to actually drive the value of the stock," he said. "A lot of the strategy that happens around investors relations has to do with scheduling and when you announce certain things and so how do you do it when your stock is being traded 24/7?" watch now VIDEO 2:22 02:22 Why Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo expects more companies to embrace tokenization efforts Crypto "The executives were actually quite excited about this new innovation and potentially getting more interest into the stock. It was really from the [investor relations] side that they received push back," and heard "let's hold off," Grushkowsky added. The lack of awareness may even extend to executives overseeing digital asset initiatives, suggesting that some rejections stem from internal communication gaps and unfamiliarity with the process, according to Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo, whose company is one of the first being listed on OKX. Securitize is also the tokenization partner for OKX. "We've talked to some of the issuers that have opted out [where] the head of digital assets doesn't even know who in the company rejected them," he said. "This is a consequence of, first, the novelty of the process and of these venues, and second, the lack of understanding of what they're being notified to do." watch now VIDEO 3:05 03:05 Robinhood CEO on tokenization: It allows us to distribute access to U.S. stocks globally Squawk Box Despite the initial pushback, Domingo expects more issuers to participate as companies become more familiar with the model, noting that some regulated trading venues can operate without issuer consent. Long game Company objections raise a separate question about which of the different tokenization models will prove most attractive. The main alternative to the OKXICE model is an issuer-led approach that integrates blockchain-based shares into existing regulated market infrastructures, with issuers retaining greater control over the process. Bullish, a digital asset platform, is pursuing an example of this model through its partnership with Equiniti, the transfer-agent business it's acquiring for $4 billion . Nasdaq's planned launch of an issuer-centric tokenized equities model in partnership with Kraken parent Payward in the second quarter of next year could offer a test of that framework and whether companies are more willing to embrace tokenization under a different structure. Nasdaq and the New York Stock Exchange, owned by Intercontinental, and others are responding to a structural shift in how securities are issued, traded and settled. Tokenization has become attractive to institutions and investors because it enables round the clock stock trading, shortened settlement times, fractional ownership and eases the use of securities as collateral. watch now VIDEO 11:31 11:31 How big banks like JPMorgan and Citi want to put Wall Street on a blockchain Crypto World For the exchanges, it presents a way to keep control of trading and market infrastructure as crypto-native, blockchain-based venues seek to bring traditional financial assets on to blockchain. It's a long way off before it becomes a meaningful revenue driver, however, according to Clear Street analyst Owen Lau. "It increases the [total addressable market], that's the number one thing," Lau said. "In the near term, there may not be enough of an incremental revenue opportunity, but the trend is there. headlines.title: Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ sparks FTX portrayal debate among crypto bigwigs from CZ to Star Xu
headlines.summary: Netflix’s "The Altruists" has drawn backlash over its portrayal of the FTX collapse, with prominent crypto industry figures questioning the series’ accuracy
headlines.article_text: Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ sparks debates over depiction of FTX collapse Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Netflix’s portrayal of the FTX collapse has drawn criticism from Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao and other crypto industry figures. The series misrepresents the roles of key figures in the FTX scandal, critics say. Netflix has previously faced defamation lawsuits over its portrayals of real-life figures in "Inventing Anna" and "Baby Reindeer." In this article NFLX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT NEW YORK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 19: (L-R) Anthony Boyle, Julia Garner and Graham Moore attend Netflix's "The Altruists" New York Premiere at The Plaza Hotel on November 19, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Arturo Holmes/WireImage) Arturo Holmes | Wireimage | Getty Images Netflix's "The Altruists," released Nov. 19, has sparked backlash from prominent cryptocurrency industry figures, including Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, over its portrayal of the collapse of FTX. Critics have questioned the accuracy of the series' portrayal of the FTX collapse, particularly how it assigns responsibility of the scandal. Several crypto industry figures argue that it softens the culpability of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison while casting Zhao — widely known as CZ — as an outsized villain. Zhao criticized the series in a post on X , calling it "insane" and questioning whether the show was intended to influence public perception. He declined to comment to CNBC beyond his social-media posts. Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program at Binance, in violation of the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act, in a case separate from the FTX fraud. He was sentenced to four months in prison in 2024 and pardoned by President Donald Trump in October 2025. FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022 after a liquidity crisis exposed deep financial problems at the exchange. Investigations later found that billions of dollars in customer funds had been diverted to Alameda Research . Shortly before FTX's collapse, Zhao announced that Binance would liquidate its remaining holdings of FTT, FTX's native token, intensifying pressure on the exchange. Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison in March 2024 after being convicted of fraud and conspiracy charges. Ellison pleaded guilty to fraud and conspiracy, and later cooperated with prosecutors, according to the Justice Department. Crypto commentator Kaleo wrote on X that the series portrayed Bankman-Fried and Ellison as having been pressured and groomed by Zhao into committing their alleged crimes, while casting Zhao as the figure who orchestrated the scandal. "Whoever wrote this script is shameless," Kaleo added. He identifies himself as a co-founder of NFT project LedgArt. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin said in a reply on X that the show exaggerated Zhao's accent to the point of raising questions about whether the portrayal was racist. Meanwhile, Tigran Gambaryan, a former Binance executive and U.S. federal agent, commented on LinkedIn that the series downplayed Bankman-Fried's responsibility while portraying Zhao as a "cartoonish villain," undermining the showrunners' credibility. Binance co-founder Yi He criticized the series for portraying its characters as "one-dimensional" and "stereotyped," while suggesting that it shifted blame away from those responsible for FTX's collapse. She compared the show unfavorably with Chinese short-form drama platform Hongguo, saying Netflix "might as well be canceled." Changpeng Zhao, co-founder of Binance Holdings Ltd., during the Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, China, on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. Chan Long Hei | Bloomberg | Getty Images But the reactions were not uniformly supportive of Zhao. In a post on X , OKX founder Star Xu said that rather than dismissing criticism as coordinated attacks by competitors, Zhao should respond with facts and evidence. Xu was responding to a post questioning whether accounts defending Zhao were part of a bot network. The eight-episode drama stars Anthony Boyle as FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, Julia Garner as former Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison and Terry Chen as Zhao. Netflix did not respond to a request for comment. In an interview published by Netflix before the series' release, Graham Moore, the show's creator and co-showrunner, said he encouraged the actors to develop fully three-dimensional characters rather than simply imitate the real-life figures they portrayed. Speaking to Business Insider, Moore said, "I can never prove what was going on in the hearts or minds of Sam's friends when they made those decisions." Moore said he drew on extensive research into the real-life figures' backgrounds and public statements to imagine what may have driven the fractures between them. "The story we're telling is not a financial story, and it's not a crypto story. It's a deeply personal story," he added. Netflix legal disputes While criticism of "The Altruists" has so far unfolded largely on social media, Netflix has previously faced defamation lawsuits over dramatizations of real-life events, including "Inventing Anna" and "Baby Reindeer." Rachel DeLoache Williams, a former Vanity Fair photo editor, sued Netflix in 2022 over her portrayal in "Inventing Anna," a series about convicted fraudster Anna Sorokin. Williams alleged that the show used her real name and personal details while falsely depicting her as greedy, dishonest and disloyal, including portraying her as exploiting her friendship with Sorokin for financial gain. The lawsuit was dismissed in February 2026 after the parties reached a settlement. Netflix and Williams' attorney reportedly confirmed the settlement in separate statements, saying, "Williams and Netflix have resolved the lawsuit." In 2024, Fiona Harvey, who said she inspired the character Martha in "Baby Reindeer," sued Netflix for at least $170 million. Harvey alleged that the series falsely portrayed her as a convicted stalker who had served time in prison and sexually assaulted the show's creator, Richard Gadd. The case is reportedly scheduled to go to trial in May 2027. "We intend to defend this matter vigorously and to stand by Richard Gadd's right to tell his story," Netflix said in a statement reported by the Associated Press. She also challenged the show's claim to be based on a true story and alleged that viewers were able to identify her as the character depicted. headlines.title: Investors give a thumbs down to Tata Steel-APL Apollo $1.67 billion deal, plunging shares
headlines.summary: Tata Steel will buy a 26.4% stake in India's leading structural steel pipes and tubes maker to boost downstream capacity.
headlines.article_text: Tata Steel shares drop as it seeks to by $1.67 billion stake in APL Apollo Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tata Steel will buy a 26.4% stake in APL Apollo for 2,100 rupees per share. Tata Steel will ​also make an open offer to acquire an additional 26% ‌stake, which, if successful, would take its stake to 52.38% World’s second-largest steel maker ArcelorMittal was also reportedly in the fray to acquire India’s leading structural steel pipes and tubes maker. In this article TATASTEEL-IN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A general view of Tata Steel steelworks on March 27, 2018 in Port Talbot, United Kingdom. Matthew Horwood | Getty Images Tata Steel , one of the world's leading steel producers, on Monday said it will buy a 26.4% stake in India's largest structural steel pipe and tube maker, APL Apollo , for 155.1 billion rupees ($1.67 billion). The acquisition will boost Tata Steel's downstream integration to around 53% from 35%, the company said in a stock exchange filing. That will lead to more value addition, improved product mix, and greater exposure to higher-margin downstream segments, it said. Investors reacted negatively to the deal, with shares of Tata Steel sliding over 9% on Monday, while APL Apollo's stock crashed more than 19% . While the deal is likely to be positive in the long term, the complex structure and lack of clarity have rattled investors, Deven Choksey, founder and managing director of wealth management firm DRChoksey FinServ, told CNBC. As per Tata Steel, before acquiring APL Apollo, it will sell its steel tubes business and Tata Steel Colors to APL Apollo for 280 billion rupees. "APL Apollo will initially fund the acquisition through a mix of acquisition financing and subsequently replace the debt with long-term capitalization," Tata Steel said. "The deal is appearing very complex," said Choksey, adding that minority investors have not been given any clarity or taken into consideration while signing this deal. Tata Steel will hold an investor call, post-market hours on Monday. APL Apollo said after the deal it plans to more than double the downstream capacity to 15.5 million tons from the current 7.5 million tons, making it a leading global downstream steel firm. This capacity addition will be completed by 2035 and would include around 9 million tons per annum of steel tubes and around 6.5 million tons per annum of color-coated products, as per Tata Steel. Tata Steel will acquire a stake from existing shareholders of APL Apollo for 2,100 rupees per share and will ​also make an open offer to acquire an additional 26% ‌stake for 2,301.40 rupees a piece. If the open offer is successful, Tata Steel would get a controlling stake of 52.38% in APL Apollo. World's second-largest steel maker ArcelorMittal was also reportedly in the fray to acquire APL Apollo. The acquisition of APL Apollo would "create a downstream powerhouse for the future" that will serve the growing Indian market, T V Narendran, chief executive and managing director of Tata Steel, said in the release. Tata Steel, which has an annual crude steel capacity of over 35 million tons per annum, is one of the world's most geographically diversified steel producers with presence across India, Europe and Thailand .
